questions.question: A scientist is testing an unknown powder. She adds it to an acid and finds that a chemical reaction occurs, forming water and a compound called a salt. Based on this observation, what category of substance must the powder be?
options: An alkali only, because all salts are made by alkalis
A base, because it reacted with the acid to form a salt
A metal element, because only pure metals can form salts with acids
An indicator, because it changed the nature of the acid

questions.question: Copper(II) oxide and sodium hydroxide are both bases. When added to water, copper(II) oxide does not dissolve, whereas sodium hydroxide dissolves completely. What can be correctly concluded about these two substances?
options: Both substances are alkalis because they are both bases.
Copper(II) oxide is an alkali, but sodium hydroxide is not.
Sodium hydroxide is an alkali, but copper(II) oxide is not.
Neither substance is an alkali because alkalis must be acids.

questions.question: A student has two unlabelled beakers, one containing an acid and the other containing an alkali. Which of the following experimental procedures would successfully identify which beaker contains the alkali?
options: Dip blue litmus paper into a beaker; if it remains blue, that beaker must contain the alkali.
Dip red litmus paper into a beaker; if it turns blue, that beaker contains the alkali.
Dip red litmus paper into a beaker; if it remains red, that beaker contains the alkali.
Dip blue litmus paper into a beaker; if it turns red, that beaker contains the alkali.

questions.question: If a piece of magnesium ribbon is dropped into a beaker of dilute sulfuric acid, bubbles are seen rising through the liquid. What are the products of this reaction?
options: Magnesium sulfate and hydrogen gas
Magnesium oxide and water
Magnesium hydroxide and oxygen gas
Magnesium carbonate and carbon dioxide gas

questions.question: A student writes down a word equation to represent the reaction between zinc and hydrochloric acid: 'zinc + hydrochloric acid -> zinc chloride'. What is incorrect about this word equation?
options: The reactant should be zinc oxide, not zinc.
The products should include water as well as zinc chloride.
The products must include hydrogen gas in addition to zinc chloride.
The name of the salt produced should be zinc chlorate, not zinc chloride.

questions.question: During an experiment reacting iron with hydrochloric acid, a student wants to confirm that the gas collected in a test tube is hydrogen. What is the correct procedure and result for this test?
options: Introduce a glowing splint into the test tube; it will relight.
Introduce a lit splint into the test tube; it will make a squeaky pop.
Bubble the gas through limewater; the limewater will turn cloudy.
Hold damp blue litmus paper in the gas; it will turn red.

questions.question: When calcium carbonate powder is added to dilute nitric acid, rapid fizzing is observed. Which of the following lists all the products formed in this reaction?
options: Calcium nitrate, water, and carbon dioxide
Calcium nitride and hydrogen
Calcium oxide and carbon dioxide
Calcium nitrate and hydrogen carbonate

questions.question: A student is investigating the reaction between copper carbonate and sulfuric acid. To prove that carbon dioxide gas is being released, which method should they use?
options: Hold a lit splint at the mouth of the tube and listen for a squeaky pop.
Hold damp red litmus paper in the gas and watch for it to turn blue.
Bubble the gas through limewater and observe if it turns cloudy.
Place a glowing splint in the gas and see if it relights.

questions.question: An ancient marble statue has been standing outdoors in an industrial city for decades. Over time, the details on the statue's face have become worn away. Which chemical explanation best describes this process?
options: Acid rain reacts with the marble to produce a salt, water, and carbon dioxide, gradually consuming the statue's material.
Acid rain deposits a layer of metal oxide on the marble, which blocks the details from being seen.
Pure water dissolves the marble to produce hydrogen gas and calcium hydroxide.
Acid rain reacts with marble to form a highly concentrated acid coating that neutralises the stone.

questions.question: Which of the following word equations correctly represents a general neutralisation reaction between a base and an acid?
options: base + acid -> metal salt + hydrogen
base + acid -> metal salt + water
base + acid -> metal carbonate + water
base + acid -> non-metal oxide + hydrogen

questions.question: A student mixes aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous hydrochloric acid together. What are the correct chemical formulas for these two starting reactants?
options: NaH(aq) and HClO(aq)
NaOH(aq) and HCl(aq)
NaOH(s) and HCl(g)
Na2O(aq) and H2Cl(aq)

questions.question: If potassium hydroxide (a base) reacts with sulfuric acid, what is the name of the metal salt that is formed?
options: Potassium sulfate
Potassium chloride
Potassium sulfur
Hydrogen sulfate

questions.question: A student is asked to classify several chemical compounds. Which of the following groups contains only compounds that are classified as bases?
options: Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide
Copper oxide and sodium hydroxide
Sodium chloride and copper sulfate
Carbon dioxide and water

questions.question: Magnesium oxide is added to a beaker of dilute hydrochloric acid. What role does the magnesium oxide play in this chemical reaction?
options: It acts as an acid to lower the pH of the mixture.
It acts as a base and reacts with the acid to neutralise it.
It acts as an indicator to show when the reaction has finished.
It acts as a solvent to dissolve the hydrochloric acid.

questions.question: Sulfur dioxide is a non-metal oxide gas. If sulfur dioxide gas is bubbled into a beaker of pure water and a few drops of universal indicator are added, what will be observed?
options: The solution will remain neutral with a pH of 7 because sulfur is not a metal.
The solution will become alkaline because non-metal oxides form basic solutions.
The solution will become acidic because non-metal oxides dissolved in water form acidic solutions.
The solution will become a solid salt because non-metals react with water to form precipitates.

questions.question: Solution A has a much higher concentration of hydrogen than Solution B. What can we conclude about their respective pH values?
options: Solution A has a lower pH than Solution B.
Solution A has a higher pH than Solution B.
Both solutions will have the exact same pH.
Solution A must have a pH of 14, while Solution B has a pH of 7.

questions.question: A solution of hydrochloric acid has a pH of 4. Water is evaporated from the solution until its hydrogen concentration increases by a factor of 100. What is the new pH of the solution?
options: pH 6
pH 2
pH 3
pH 5

questions.question: Three solutions have pH values of 1.5, 7.0, and 12.5 respectively. How should these solutions be classified?
options: pH 1.5 is alkaline, pH 7.0 is neutral, pH 12.5 is acidic.
pH 1.5 is acidic, pH 7.0 is alkaline, pH 12.5 is neutral.
pH 1.5 is acidic, pH 7.0 is neutral, pH 12.5 is alkaline.
All three solutions are acidic because they contain hydrogen.

questions.question: A student extracts juice from a red cabbage to use as a natural pH indicator. They test three unknown liquids and observe the following colours: Liquid X turns pink, Liquid Y turns purple, and Liquid Z turns green. What are the natures of these liquids?
options: Liquid X is neutral, Liquid Y is alkaline, Liquid Z is acidic.
Liquid X is alkaline, Liquid Y is acidic, Liquid Z is neutral.
Liquid X is acidic, Liquid Y is neutral, Liquid Z is alkaline.
Liquid X is acidic, Liquid Y is alkaline, Liquid Z is neutral.

questions.question: Why is universal indicator often preferred over litmus paper when investigating the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali?
options: Litmus paper only works for weak acids, whereas universal indicator only works for strong alkalis.
Universal indicator turns many different colours depending on pH, allowing the gradual change in pH to be monitored.
Universal indicator acts as a reactant to speed up the neutralisation process.
Litmus paper changes colour too slowly, whereas universal indicator changes colour instantly and permanently.

questions.question: An industrial waste pipe releases a solution with a pH of 3. After treatment, the pH of the effluent is measured at pH 6. How has the acidity (concentration of hydrogen ions) of the solution changed?
options: It is 3 times less acidic.
It is 30 times less acidic.
It is 1,000 times less acidic.
It is 10,000 times less acidic.

questions.question: A student neutralises potassium hydroxide with sulfuric acid. What is the correct name of the salt produced in this chemical reaction?
options: Potassium sulfate
Potassium chloride
Potassium hydroxide sulfate
Sulfuric potassium

questions.question: A scientist adds hydrochloric acid to a sample of solid copper carbonate in a sealed flask connected to a gas syringe. Which of the following correctly describes what they will observe and the substances present in the flask after the reaction is complete?
options: No bubbles form because copper is unreactive, leaving the copper carbonate solid unchanged.
Effervescence occurs, and the products left in the flask are copper chloride, water, and carbon dioxide gas.
The solid dissolves with no gas produced, forming a solution of copper chloride and water.
Effervescence occurs, leaving only water and a precipitate of copper metal in the flask.

questions.question: Solution A has a hydrogen ion concentration that is 100 times greater than Solution B. Solution B has a pH of 5. What is the pH of Solution A, and why?
options: pH 7, because higher hydrogen concentration increases the potential of hydrogen.
pH 3, because higher hydrogen concentration results in a lower pH value.
pH 5.2, because concentration changes have a minimal linear effect on pH.
pH 1, because hydrogen concentration is inversely proportional by a factor of 100 directly.

questions.question: A historic building made of marble (calcium carbonate) is exposed to acid rain (containing sulfuric acid) over many decades. Which of the following best explains why the building's details are eroding?
options: The acid rain dissolves the marble to form soluble calcium sulfate, water, and carbon dioxide gas, which escape.
The acid rain causes a physical erosion process by freezing inside the pores of the marble.
The acid rain neutralises the marble, turning it into a highly reactive metal that burns in air.
The acid rain reacts with the marble to form insoluble calcium oxide which flakes off as a green powder.

questions.question: A student is testing three unlabeled liquids: X, Y, and Z. Liquid X turns red cabbage indicator red. Liquid Y turns it green. Liquid Z is a mixture of X and Y in exact neutralisation proportions. What colour will the red cabbage indicator turn when added to Liquid Z?
options: Pink
Green
Purple
Colourless

questions.question: In the chemical equation: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> MgCl2(aq) + H2(g), what do the state symbols tell us about the reaction mixture?
options: Magnesium starts as a liquid, hydrochloric acid is a gas, and the salt is a solid.
Magnesium is a solid, hydrochloric acid is dissolved in water, and hydrogen is released as a gas.
Magnesium is soluble, hydrochloric acid is aqueous, and hydrogen is a liquid.
Magnesium is a solid, hydrochloric acid is a gas, and the reaction occurs without water.

questions.question: A technician wants to write the word equation for the reaction of zinc with nitric acid. What are the correct reactants and products?
options: zinc + nitric acid -> zinc nitrate + water
zinc + nitric acid -> zinc oxide + nitrogen gas
zinc + nitric acid -> zinc nitrate + hydrogen
zinc + nitric acid -> zinc nitride + hydrogen oxide

questions.question: When sulfur dioxide gas (a non-metal oxide) is bubbled through a beaker of pure water containing universal indicator, what colour change would you expect to observe?
options: From green to red or orange, because non-metal oxides form acidic solutions.
From green to blue or purple, because non-metal oxides form alkaline solutions.
The solution remains green because non-metal oxides do not react with water.
From red to green, because the non-metal oxide neutralises the water.

questions.question: During an experiment, a student bubbles an unknown gas through limewater, and the limewater remains completely clear. However, a lit splint placed in the gas goes out immediately. What can the student conclude about the gas?
options: The gas is definitely carbon dioxide because it extinguished the lit splint.
The gas is not carbon dioxide, as carbon dioxide would have made the limewater cloudy.
The gas is hydrogen because it did not react with the limewater.
The gas is oxygen because limewater only reacts with nitrogen.

questions.question: A piece of magnesium ribbon is dropped into a beaker of hydrochloric acid. A student records three observations. Which set of observations correctly matches the expected chemical and physical changes?
options: The beaker feels cold, the metal turns green, and no bubbles are seen.
Bubbles are produced, the temperature of the beaker increases, and the magnesium ribbon gets smaller.
The magnesium ribbon expands in size, the liquid turns yellow, and the beaker cools down.
There is no change in temperature, but the metal turns into a gas and disappears instantly.

questions.question: Copper oxide is a black solid that does not dissolve in water. When warmed with dilute sulfuric acid, it reacts to form a blue solution of copper sulfate and water. What type of reaction is this?
options: Thermal decomposition, because heat was required to break down the copper oxide.
Neutralisation, because a metal oxide (base) reacts with an acid to form a salt and water.
Displacement, because copper is more reactive than hydrogen and pushes it out of the acid.
Combustion, because the oxygen in the copper oxide burns the hydrogen in the acid.

questions.question: Copper oxide and sodium hydroxide are both bases. However, copper oxide is insoluble in water, whereas sodium hydroxide dissolves easily in water. Which statement correctly compares them?
options: Both copper oxide and sodium hydroxide are alkalis.
Neither copper oxide nor sodium hydroxide are alkalis.
Copper oxide is an alkali, but sodium hydroxide is only a base.
Sodium hydroxide is an alkali, but copper oxide is not.

questions.question: You are given four substances: calcium oxide, sodium hydroxide, copper oxide, and sodium chloride. Which of these substances are classified as bases?
options: Only sodium hydroxide and sodium chloride
Calcium oxide, sodium hydroxide, and copper oxide
Only calcium oxide and copper oxide
All four substances are bases

questions.question: A chemist needs to find the exact pH value of a soil sample to one decimal place. Why would they choose a digital pH probe over universal indicator paper?
options: Universal indicator paper changes colour too slowly compared to a digital probe.
Universal indicator paper cannot measure the pH of solids, whereas a probe can.
A digital pH probe provides a precise, numerical value, whereas indicator paper relies on subjective colour matching.
Universal indicator paper only works for strong acids and strong alkalis, not weak ones.

questions.question: A bottle of concentrated sodium hydroxide solution has a hazard symbol showing a substance spilling onto a hand and eating into the skin. What safety precaution is most critical when handling this substance, and why?
options: Wear safety goggles and gloves because the substance is corrosive and can cause chemical burns.
Work in a fume cupboard because the substance is highly flammable and explosive.
Keep the bottle in a water bath because the substance will boil at room temperature.
Wear a dust mask because the liquid will evaporate into toxic solid particles.

questions.question: A student collects a gas produced from the reaction of iron with hydrochloric acid. They want to confirm if the gas is hydrogen. What should they do, and what is the expected positive result?
options: Hold a glowing splint in the gas; it should relight.
Bubble the gas through limewater; it should turn cloudy.
Introduce a lit splint to the gas; it should make a squeaky pop.
Hold damp red litmus paper in the gas; it should turn blue.

questions.question: Equal-sized pieces of magnesium, zinc, iron, and copper are added to separate test tubes containing the same volume and concentration of hydrochloric acid. Which of the following lists the metals in order of most vigorous reaction to least vigorous reaction (no reaction)?
options: Copper, Iron, Zinc, Magnesium
Magnesium, Zinc, Iron, Copper
Iron, Magnesium, Copper, Zinc
Zinc, Magnesium, Iron, Copper

questions.question: When testing a reaction between an unknown base and an acid, a student notices that a gas is produced. Can this reaction be represented by the general equation: base + acid -> metal salt + water?
options: Yes, because all neutralisation reactions produce a gas.
No, because the general equation for a base and acid reaction only produces a salt and water, meaning the base must have been a carbonate instead of a simple oxide or hydroxide.
Yes, because water evaporates to form steam, which is the gas they observed.
No, because only metals react with acids to produce salt and water.

questions.question: What is the chemical reason why all acids have a pH value below 7?
options: Acids contain oxygen atoms which make them highly reactive with water.
pH stands for 'potential of hydrogen', and acids release hydrogen ions when dissolved in water, determining their pH.
Acids contain hydroxide ions which lower the potential of hydrogen in the solution.
All acids are made of non-metal oxides which prevent hydrogen from bonding.

questions.question: A chef is experimenting with unfamiliar wild berries. They note that the juice of the berries has a distinctly sharp, sour taste. Based on this observation, what chemical component is most likely present in the berries, and how should it be classified?
options: An edible acid, which typically has a sour taste.
An alkali, which typically has a sour taste but is safe to eat.
A neutral salt, which provides the characteristic sourness of fruits.
A metal oxide, which imparts sour flavours to edible plants.

questions.question: A student is given four unlabeled powders. They are told that one of them is a chemical base. To identify which powder is the base, they mix each powder with dilute sulfuric acid. Which observation would best confirm that a powder is a base?
options: It dissolves completely in water to form a solution with a pH of 7 without reacting.
It reacts with the acid to form a compound known as a salt.
It produces bubbles of hydrogen gas when added to pure water.
It physically melts when heated but does not interact with the acid.

questions.question: Copper(II) oxide and sodium hydroxide are both classified as bases. However, only sodium hydroxide is considered an alkali. What experimental evidence explains this difference in classification?
options: Sodium hydroxide reacts with acids, whereas copper(II) oxide does not react with acids at all.
Sodium hydroxide is soluble in water, forming an alkaline solution, whereas copper(II) oxide is insoluble in water.
Copper(II) oxide contains metal atoms, while sodium hydroxide contains only non-metal atoms.
Copper(II) oxide turns universal indicator purple, while sodium hydroxide has no effect on indicators.

questions.question: A bottle of concentrated sulfuric acid and a bottle of concentrated sodium hydroxide solution both carry a hazard symbol showing a substance spilling onto a hand and eating away at the skin. What does this symbol warn users about regarding these two chemicals?
options: Both are highly flammable and will catch fire upon contact with skin.
Both are corrosive substances that can cause severe chemical burns.
Only the acid can cause damage, while the alkali is harmless but acts as a catalyst.
Both are toxic only if swallowed, but completely safe to handle with bare hands.

questions.question: A student tests a colourless liquid by dipping a piece of blue litmus paper into it, and the paper turns red. They then dip a piece of red litmus paper into a second colourless liquid, and the paper turns blue. What can be concluded about the two liquids?
options: The first liquid is neutral and the second liquid is an acid.
The first liquid is an alkali and the second liquid is an acid.
The first liquid is an acid and the second liquid is an alkali.
Both liquids are neutral, but they have different levels of dissolved oxygen.

questions.question: A piece of zinc is placed in a beaker of hydrochloric acid. Over several minutes, the student observes gas bubbles forming rapidly on the zinc, the temperature of the mixture rising, and the piece of zinc getting smaller until it can no longer be seen. Which of the following is the correct scientific interpretation of these observations?
options: A physical change occurred where the zinc melted due to the external heat of the room and dissolved.
An endothermic reaction took place, causing the zinc to absorb heat and evaporate into a gas.
An exothermic chemical reaction occurred, producing a gas and converting the solid zinc into a soluble compound.
A neutralisation reaction occurred where the acid was completely destroyed without forming any new substances.

questions.question: If a piece of magnesium metal is added to a test tube containing dilute hydrochloric acid, what are the specific chemical products formed from this reaction?
options: Magnesium chloride salt and hydrogen gas.
Magnesium oxide, water, and chlorine gas.
Magnesium hydroxide salt and water.
Carbon dioxide gas and magnesium sulfate salt.

questions.question: A student wants to represent the chemical reaction between iron and sulfuric acid using a word equation. Which of the following is the correct equation?
options: iron + sulfuric acid → iron sulfate + water
iron + sulfuric acid → iron sulfate + hydrogen
iron + sulfuric acid → iron oxide + sulfur dioxide
iron + sulfuric acid → iron hydroxide + hydrogen

questions.question: During an experiment involving a metal and an acid, a gas is collected in an inverted test tube. How can the student safely and definitively confirm that the collected gas is hydrogen?
options: Bubble the gas through limewater and observe if it turns cloudy.
Hold a glowing splint in the tube to see if it relights.
Introduce a lit splint and listen for a characteristic squeaky pop.
Use damp blue litmus paper to see if it turns red.

questions.question: When solid calcium carbonate is added to dilute nitric acid, the mixture fizzes vigorously. What are the three products of this chemical reaction?
options: Calcium nitrate, water, and hydrogen gas.
Calcium oxide, water, and carbon dioxide gas.
Calcium nitrate, water, and carbon dioxide gas.
Calcium hydroxide, nitrogen gas, and water.

questions.question: A student is investigating the reaction between copper carbonate and hydrochloric acid. They suspect that the gas being produced is carbon dioxide. How should they test this gas, and what observation would confirm their hypothesis?
options: Pass the gas through limewater; the solution should change from clear to cloudy.
Hold a lit splint at the mouth of the tube; it should produce a loud squeaky pop.
Hold a glowing splint in the gas; the splint should immediately relight.
Direct the gas onto blue litmus paper; the paper should turn blue.

questions.question: Over many decades, outdoor marble statues in industrial areas gradually lose their fine details and become pitted. Which statement best explains this phenomenon from a chemical perspective?
options: Acid rain reacts with the marble to produce a salt, water, and carbon dioxide, gradually wearing away the solid marble.
Carbon dioxide in the air directly dissolves the marble, converting it into calcium metal.
Rainwater reacts with the marble to form an insoluble protective layer of metal oxide that falls off.
The wind physically scrapes off the marble, which is a neutralisation reaction that produces hydrogen gas.

questions.question: When an insoluble metal oxide (a base) reacts with an acid, the mixture warms up and a clear solution containing a salt is formed. What is the general word equation that describes this type of neutralisation reaction?
options: base + acid → metal salt + hydrogen
base + acid → metal salt + water
metal + acid → metal salt + water + carbon dioxide
alkali + acid → metal carbonate + water

questions.question: If a chemist neutralises copper oxide (a base) using sulfuric acid, what is the name of the metal salt produced in this reaction?
options: Copper chloride
Copper sulfate
Sodium sulfate
Copper carbonate

questions.question: A teacher asks a class to identify which group of compounds are classified as common bases. Which of the following lists contains only compounds that function as bases?
options: Metal oxides and metal hydroxides
Non-metal oxides and non-metal hydroxides
Strong acids and weak acids
Hydrogen gas and carbon dioxide gas

questions.question: When black copper oxide powder is heated with dilute sulfuric acid, a blue solution of copper sulfate is formed. What is the other product of this reaction?
options: Hydrogen gas
Water
Oxygen gas
Carbon dioxide gas

questions.question: Sulfur dioxide is a gas produced by burning fossil fuels. When sulfur dioxide dissolves in water droplets in the atmosphere, what kind of solution is formed?
options: An alkaline solution, because sulfur is a non-metal.
An neutral solution, because sulfur dioxide does not react with water.
An acidic solution, because non-metal oxides form acidic solutions in water.
A highly basic solution, because sulfur dioxide is a metal oxide.

questions.question: Two beakers contain different concentrations of hydrochloric acid. Beaker A has a high concentration of hydrogen ions, while Beaker B has a very low concentration of hydrogen ions. How will their pH values compare?
options: Beaker A will have a lower pH than Beaker B.
Beaker A will have a higher pH than Beaker B.
Both beakers will have the same pH because they contain the same acid.
Beaker A will have a pH of 7, while Beaker B will have a pH of 14.

questions.question: A solution of hydrochloric acid has a pH of 4. If the concentration of hydrogen ions is increased by a factor of exactly 100, what will the new pH of the solution be?
options: pH 6
pH 2
pH 5
pH 14

questions.question: A student prepares a natural indicator using red cabbage juice. They test three unknown liquids (X, Y, and Z). Liquid X turns the indicator red, Liquid Y turns it purple, and Liquid Z turns it green. What can be concluded about the nature of these three liquids?
options: Liquid X is neutral, Liquid Y is an acid, and Liquid Z is an alkali.
Liquid X is an alkali, Liquid Y is neutral, and Liquid Z is an acid.
Liquid X is an acid, Liquid Y is neutral, and Liquid Z is an alkali.
Liquid X is an acid, Liquid Y is an alkali, and Liquid Z is neutral.

questions.question: A student measures the pH of a soil sample and finds it is pH 5. After adding a soil treatment, the pH decreases to pH 3. How has the acidity of the soil changed?
options: The soil is now 2 times more acidic.
The soil is now 20 times more acidic.
The soil is now 100 times more acidic.
The soil is now 100 times less acidic.

questions.question: If a student neutralises magnesium hydroxide with nitric acid, what is the correct name of the metal salt produced in this reaction?
options: Magnesium nitrate
Magnesium sulfate
Hydrogen nitrate
Nitric hydroxide

questions.question: A historical marble statue has slowly degraded over decades due to acid rain. Which chemical process explains this degradation?
options: Acid rain dissolves the marble without any chemical reaction, turning it into a liquid form.
Acid rain reacts with marble to produce a metal salt, water, and carbon dioxide, gradually consuming the solid marble.
Acid rain reacts with marble to produce hydrogen gas, which causes microscopic explosions on the surface.
Acid rain acts as a catalyst to turn marble into a metal oxide, which easily crumbles in the wind.

questions.question: When calcium carbonate is added to a beaker of dilute hydrochloric acid, which set of products will be formed?
options: Calcium chloride and hydrogen gas
Calcium chloride, water, and carbon dioxide
Calcium hydroxide, water, and chlorine gas
Calcium oxide, carbon dioxide, and hydrogen gas

questions.question: Solution A has a pH of 1 and Solution B has a pH of 4. Which of the following statements correctly compares the two solutions?
options: Solution A has a higher concentration of hydrogen than Solution B.
Solution B has a higher concentration of hydrogen than Solution A.
Both solutions have the same concentration of hydrogen, but Solution A is more reactive.
Solution A has no hydrogen, whereas Solution B is rich in hydrogen.

questions.question: A student extracts red cabbage juice and adds a few drops to an unknown clear solution. The mixture turns green. What does this result tell us about the unknown solution?
options: It is highly acidic.
It is neutral.
It is alkaline.
It is pure water.

questions.question: An unknown metal is placed into a beaker of sulfuric acid. The reaction produces zinc sulfate and a gas. What is the correct word equation that represents this chemical reaction?
options: zinc + sulfuric acid -> zinc sulfate + water
zinc + sulfuric acid -> zinc sulfate + hydrogen
zinc sulfate + hydrogen -> zinc + sulfuric acid
zinc oxide + sulfuric acid -> zinc sulfate + hydrogen

questions.question: In the chemical equation: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> MgCl2(aq) + H2(g), what do the state symbols (aq) and (s) represent respectively?
options: Acidic solution and solid
Aqueous (in solution) and solid
Aqua-gas and soluble
Active reactant and stable product

questions.question: Sulfur dioxide is a non-metal oxide gas produced by burning fossil fuels. When sulfur dioxide dissolves in rain droplets in the atmosphere, what kind of solution is formed and why?
options: An alkaline solution, because all non-metal oxides form hydroxides in water.
A neutral solution, because non-metal oxides do not react with water.
An acidic solution, because non-metal oxides in water make acidic solutions.
A saline solution, because non-metal oxides react with water to form salts.

questions.question: During an experiment with a metal and an acid, a student collects a gas in an inverted test tube. How can they safely confirm that the gas is hydrogen?
options: Bubble the gas through limewater and check if it turns cloudy.
Hold a glowing splint at the mouth of the tube and watch it relight.
Hold a lit splint at the mouth of the tube and listen for a squeaky pop.
Dampen blue litmus paper and place it in the tube to see if it turns red.

questions.question: To identify the gas produced when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate, a student bubbles the gas into a test tube containing a clear liquid. The liquid turns cloudy. What is the liquid, and what gas does this test confirm?
options: The liquid is limewater, and the gas is hydrogen.
The liquid is universal indicator, and the gas is oxygen.
The liquid is limewater, and the gas is carbon dioxide.
The liquid is hydrochloric acid, and the gas is carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Copper oxide is a black powder that does not dissolve in water. When heated with dilute sulfuric acid, the black powder disappears, and a blue solution is formed. What is the correct word equation for this reaction?
options: copper oxide + sulfuric acid -> copper sulfate + water
copper oxide + sulfuric acid -> copper sulfate + hydrogen
copper oxide + sulfuric acid -> copper sulfide + oxygen
copper oxide + sulfuric acid -> copper sulfate + carbon dioxide + water

questions.question: A beaker contains an unknown liquid. A student dips blue litmus paper into the liquid, and it remains blue. They then dip red litmus paper into the same liquid, and it turns blue. What can the student conclude about the liquid?
options: The liquid is highly acidic.
The liquid is neutral.
The liquid is alkaline.
The liquid is pure water.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a base and an alkali?
options: Bases turn litmus paper red, while alkalis turn litmus paper blue.
Alkalis are bases that can dissolve in water, whereas some bases are insoluble.
Alkalis react with metals to produce hydrogen, while bases do not react with metals.
Bases are highly corrosive, whereas alkalis are completely safe to touch.

questions.question: A student is writing a summary of neutralisation reactions. Which general word equation should they use to represent a neutralisation reaction between a base and an acid?
options: base + acid -> metal salt + hydrogen
base + acid -> metal salt + water
base + acid -> metal salt + carbon dioxide + water
base + acid -> non-metal oxide + water

questions.question: When a small strip of magnesium ribbon is dropped into a test tube containing hydrochloric acid, several observations are made. Which of the following is NOT an observation associated with this reaction?
options: Bubbles of gas are produced rapidly in the mixture.
The test tube feels warm to the touch.
The magnesium ribbon gradually reduces in size and disappears.
A white solid precipitate forms and falls to the bottom of the tube.

questions.question: Three different metals (X, Y, and Z) are added to separate test tubes containing dilute hydrochloric acid. Metal X produces bubbles rapidly; metal Y shows no reaction at all; metal Z produces bubbles very slowly. What is the correct order of these metals from most reactive to least reactive?
options: Y, Z, X
X, Z, Y
X, Y, Z
Z, X, Y

questions.question: Sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) is often used in neutralisation experiments. What is the composition of the carbonate group found in this compound?
options: One carbon atom and two oxygen atoms bonded together.
One carbon atom and three oxygen atoms bonded together.
Three carbon atoms and one oxygen atom bonded together.
One calcium atom and three oxygen atoms bonded together.

questions.question: A teacher asks the class to select two compounds that belong to the group known as common bases. Which pair should the students choose?
options: Hydrochloric acid and sodium chloride
Copper oxide and sodium hydroxide
Carbon dioxide and water
Magnesium metal and hydrogen gas

questions.question: A student wants to find the exact pH value of a solution to one decimal place. Why would they choose a pH meter (a digital sensor) over litmus paper or red cabbage indicator?
options: Litmus paper only shows if a substance is acidic or alkaline, and red cabbage indicator cannot be used with liquids.
Red cabbage indicator changes color too slowly, while litmus paper is highly toxic to handle.
Chemical indicators only provide broad color ranges or binary results, whereas a pH meter can provide precise, numerical measurements.
A pH meter is the only indicator that can detect whether a solution contains hydrogen.
